topic: Universities should replace written examinations with project-based assessment.
argument: Universities should replace exams with projects. A 2021 study found project-based courses improved retention, so assessment should follow the way students learn best. Some argue projects are harder to grade fairly, but clear rubrics address that. This approach works.
notes: The case is developed, but it presents the approach as generally effective without stating the conditions or limits under which it works.

topic: Social media should be banned for children under 16.
argument: All social media is harmful and nobody benefits from it in any way.
notes: The absolute claim that nobody benefits from any social media is too broad to defend.

topic: Universities should replace written examinations with project-based assessment.
argument: Projects are never a fair way to assess anyone because every group project is dominated by one student.
notes: The claim that projects are never fair and every group project is dominated by one student is absolute and overbroad.

topic: Governments should regulate the use of generative AI tools.
argument: Governments should regulate generative AI. Deepfakes caused documented election disinformation in several countries, so labelling rules would reduce harm. Critics argue regulation slows innovation, but narrow labelling rules leave research untouched. These rules will stop all misuse.
notes: The claim that the proposed rules will stop all misuse is an indefensible absolute.

topic: Remote learning is more effective than traditional classroom learning.
argument: My cousin did an online course and failed it, so remote learning clearly does not work for students.
notes: One person's failed online course is used to draw a conclusion about remote learning for students generally; this is a hasty generalisation.

topic: Governments should regulate the use of generative AI tools.
argument: My favourite holiday destination is Sri Lanka because of its beaches and tea hills.
notes: A personal preference about a holiday destination does not address whether governments should regulate generative AI.

topic: Artificial intelligence should be used to grade student assignments.
argument: AI should grade assignments because it will make marking better for everyone involved.
notes: The argument asserts that AI will improve marking for everyone but supplies no specific evidence, example, or source.

topic: Remote learning is more effective than traditional classroom learning.
argument: Remote learning is not more effective. A 2020 meta-analysis found lower engagement online, which suggests students absorb less. Supporters point to flexibility, though flexibility alone does not produce learning.
notes: The argument treats lower engagement as a general indicator of poorer learning without identifying contexts or students for whom the finding may not apply.

topic: Remote learning is more effective than traditional classroom learning.
argument: Remote learning is not more effective, classrooms simply work better for students.
notes: The claim that classrooms work better is unsupported by a specific reason, example, or source.

topic: Artificial intelligence should be used to grade student assignments.
argument: AI grading is kind of interesting for education and stuff.
notes: The wording is too vague to establish a clear position about whether or how AI should grade assignments.

topic: Governments should regulate the use of generative AI tools.
argument: All regulation of technology always fails, so governments should never try to regulate generative AI.
notes: The claims that all technology regulation always fails and governments should never regulate are absolute.

topic: Governments should regulate the use of generative AI tools.
argument: Generative AI should be regulated. Studies show synthetic media is hard to detect, so labelling rules would protect voters from deception.
notes: The argument gives a reason for regulation but does not address the likely opposing concern that regulation may restrict innovation.

topic: Remote learning is more effective than traditional classroom learning.
argument: Remote learning is always better and every student learns more at home than anywhere else.
notes: The words 'always' and 'every student' make an excessively broad claim about remote learning.

topic: Universities should replace written examinations with project-based assessment.
argument: Assessment methods are a complicated issue with many sides.
notes: It says the issue has many sides but does not state a definite position on the motion.

topic: Governments should regulate the use of generative AI tools.
argument: Governments should regulate generative AI because everyone knows that unregulated technology always leads to disaster.
notes: The assertion that unregulated technology always leads to disaster is an unsupported absolute generalisation.

topic: Remote learning is more effective than traditional classroom learning.
argument: Classroom learning is more effective. Research shows face-to-face contact improves attention and feedback speed, so students learn more in person.
notes: The argument offers relevant support for classroom learning but does not engage with reasons in favour of remote learning.

topic: Governments should regulate the use of generative AI tools.
argument: Governments should regulate generative AI. Deepfakes affected election campaigns in several countries according to news reports.
notes: The reference to deepfakes affecting elections does not explain why that evidence supports government regulation or what regulation would achieve.

topic: Universities should replace written examinations with project-based assessment.
argument: Project-based assessment is better. Football clubs in Europe earned 29 billion euros in 2022 according to a report.
notes: Football-club revenue has no meaningful connection to the merits of project-based university assessment.

topic: Universities should replace written examinations with project-based assessment.
argument: Football is the most popular sport in the world and millions of people watch it every weekend.
notes: The statement about football popularity does not address the debate over replacing written examinations.

topic: Artificial intelligence should be used to grade student assignments.
argument: AI grading should be adopted. Trials at several universities cut marking time by 40%, so lecturers can spend that time giving personal feedback to students.
notes: The efficiency evidence supports AI grading, but the argument does not address concerns such as bias or reliability.

topic: Artificial intelligence should be used to grade student assignments.
argument: AI should not grade student work. A 2023 study found large language models disagreed with teachers on 30% of essays.
notes: The reported disagreement rate is not connected explicitly to why AI should not grade student work or what level of disagreement is unacceptable.

topic: Governments should regulate the use of generative AI tools.
argument: Governments should not regulate generative AI. Evidence from the early internet suggests light-touch rules supported rapid innovation, so heavy regulation risks slowing useful tools.
notes: The innovation argument is supported by an example, but it does not address the opposing case for safeguards against AI-related harms.

topic: Artificial intelligence should be used to grade student assignments.
argument: AI should never grade student work because every AI system is always biased and teachers are always fair.
notes: The repeated claims that every AI system is always biased and teachers are always fair are absolute and indefensible.

topic: Artificial intelligence should be used to grade student assignments.
argument: AI should not grade assignments. The Eiffel Tower receives about seven million visitors every year according to tourism data.
notes: Tourism figures for the Eiffel Tower do not support a position on AI grading.

topic: Universities should replace written examinations with project-based assessment.
argument: Many universities have beautiful campuses with large libraries and sports grounds that attract international students.
notes: Campus attractiveness and facilities do not address whether examinations should be replaced with project-based assessment.

topic: Universities should replace written examinations with project-based assessment.
argument: Project-based assessment is better than exams because students learn more from projects.
notes: The argument gives a reason but provides no specific evidence, example, or source to support the claim that students learn more from projects.

topic: Social media should be banned for children under 16.
argument: Banning social media for under-16s is unnecessary. A 2022 survey found 60% of teenagers spend under two hours a day online.
notes: The survey statistic about time spent online does not explain why a ban is unnecessary or how that usage level bears on the risks of social media.

topic: Remote learning is more effective than traditional classroom learning.
argument: Remote learning is more effective than classroom learning. According to a survey, 70% of students saved two hours of commuting per day.
notes: Saving commuting time is relevant to convenience, but the argument does not explain how it demonstrates greater learning effectiveness.

topic: Social media should be banned for children under 16.
argument: It should be banned because it is harmful.
notes: The pronoun 'it' and the general statement that something is harmful leave the position and its supporting reason insufficiently specified.

topic: Universities should replace written examinations with project-based assessment.
argument: Exams are just not great things.
notes: The phrase 'not great things' is too vague to identify a precise criticism of written examinations.

topic: Artificial intelligence should be used to grade student assignments.
argument: If we allow AI to grade one essay then soon teachers will be replaced and education will collapse.
notes: It predicts teacher replacement and educational collapse from allowing one AI-graded essay, which is a slippery-slope argument.

topic: Social media should be banned for children under 16.
argument: Social media is bad.
notes: The statement that social media is bad gives no clear, developed claim about the proposed ban or the specific harm at issue.

topic: Social media should be banned for children under 16.
argument: Children under 16 should not use social media. A 2019 study of 12000 teenagers found heavy use linked to higher depression rates. Therefore a minimum age is justified.
notes: The association between heavy use and depression is not enough by itself to establish why a minimum age is the appropriate policy response.

topic: Universities should replace written examinations with project-based assessment.
argument: Written exams should stay. Evidence from several studies shows recall under time pressure predicts later performance, so exams measure something valuable. Defenders of projects say exams cause stress, but stress is manageable with support.
notes: The argument presents timed recall and support for managing exam stress as broadly sufficient, without qualifying the types of learning or students for which exams are suitable.

topic: Social media should be banned for children under 16.
argument: Children and phones are a thing we should think about more.
notes: The statement is tentative and vague; it does not make a clear argument for or against the proposed ban.

topic: Universities should replace written examinations with project-based assessment.
argument: Written exams should stay. Surveys show that 80% of employers have used timed written tests in hiring.
notes: Employer use of timed tests does not establish that written university examinations are educationally valuable or should remain.

topic: Artificial intelligence should be used to grade student assignments.
argument: AI should grade assignments. Trials in three universities cut marking time by 40%, so teachers can give more feedback. Critics fear bias, but audits can detect it. It improves education.
notes: The argument generalises from a small set of trials to a broad claim that AI grading improves education, without specifying limits or conditions.

topic: Remote learning is more effective than traditional classroom learning.
argument: Classroom learning is more effective. Coffee consumption among adults rose by 12% in the last decade according to a market report.
notes: Adult coffee-consumption trends do not support the claim that classroom learning is more effective.

topic: Artificial intelligence should be used to grade student assignments.
argument: Electric cars are the future of transport because they reduce fuel costs and emissions.
notes: The argument about electric cars does not address the motion on AI grading of student assignments.

topic: Remote learning is more effective than traditional classroom learning.
argument: Cats are better pets than dogs because they are cleaner and more independent.
notes: The comparison of cats and dogs is unrelated to the effectiveness of remote learning.

topic: Social media should be banned for children under 16.
argument: Social media should be banned for children. The number of smartphones sold last year reached a record high, which shows the market is big.
notes: High smartphone sales show market size, not why social media should be banned for children.

topic: Remote learning is more effective than traditional classroom learning.
argument: Remote learning must be better because most universities moved online during the pandemic and so many people cannot be wrong.
notes: The claim that many universities moved online and 'so many people cannot be wrong' relies on popularity as proof (bandwagon reasoning).

topic: Governments should regulate the use of generative AI tools.
argument: Generative AI should not be regulated because regulation would hurt innovation.
notes: The argument asserts that regulation would hurt innovation but gives no specific evidence, example, or source.

topic: Social media should be banned for children under 16.
argument: Banning social media is wrong because only idiots think children cannot manage their own screen time.
notes: Calling opponents idiots attacks people rather than addressing the reasons for or against a ban (ad hominem).

topic: Governments should regulate the use of generative AI tools.
argument: Governments should regulate generative AI. The moon landing in 1969 involved over 400000 engineers.
notes: The number of engineers involved in the moon landing does not support the case for regulating generative AI.
